Low-upkeep turf for Oak Ridge's rental-heavy blocks

Long-term landlords and homeowners across Oak Ridge's 1950s through 1980s subdivisions pay the same $8–$18 a square foot as the rest of Central Florida for a turf conversion, a range that has not moved since our September 2026 check, typically settling at $10–$16. What differs block to block is whether the lot is owner-occupied or a rental turning over every lease term.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

A 520 sq ft yard behind a rental duplex

Say you have a 520 sq ft yard behind one side of a 1962 duplex held as a long-term rental, with the other unit's tenant sharing the driveway but not the backyard. At the published range that prices between $4,160 and $9,360, with most jobs this size landing near $5,200 to $8,320. For a landlord, the calculation usually weighs that cost against several years of re-sodding a lawn that a rotating set of tenants never waters on schedule, rather than against a single season's water bill the way an owner-occupant might.

A yard that survives one tenant after another

A rental lawn takes a different kind of wear than an owner-occupied one: irregular mowing between leases, a moving truck parked on the grass, a tenant's dog that the lease did not mention. Synthetic turf does not care about any of that in the way St. Augustine does, since there is no mowing schedule to fall behind on and no root system to compact under a truck's tires. For a landlord holding a house or a duplex unit long-term, that translates to one line item that stops recurring between tenants rather than a lawn that needs re-sodding every time a lease ends badly. The full installation breakdown covers what the base and turf actually consist of, regardless of who ends up living behind it.

What the residential price range buys in Oak Ridge

Installed synthetic lawn runs eight to eighteen dollars a square foot, with most yards landing between ten and sixteen. That range covers more than the turf roll itself: base material, compaction labor, seam tape and adhesive, and edge anchoring all sit inside the same number, and turf is typically under half of the total cost on a Oak Ridge job. Paying toward the lower end of the range usually means a lighter product on a straightforward, flat, easy-access yard, while the upper end reflects a heavier face weight, tighter stitching, or a lot with tricky access that slows the crew down regardless of which product goes on top.

Duplex and side-by-side lots split the job, not the price

A duplex or a side-by-side rental shares one property line down the middle, which changes how a crew lays out seams and edging more than it changes the total cost. Turf on both sides usually gets run as one continuous job rather than two separate small ones, with the dividing seam kept a foot or two off the actual property line so a future dispute over lawn care never becomes a boundary argument. Where two units carry separate water meters, capping irrigation heads on each side still happens independently, since the state's rule against watering synthetic turf applies meter by meter, not lot by lot.

What washed crushed rock does that unwashed fill can't

The state's turf rule specifically requires the crushed rock or crushed concrete under a lawn to be washed before it goes in, and there's a reason beyond paperwork. Unwashed material carries fine dust and clay particles that settle into the gaps between the larger stones once they get wet, and over a season or two those fines bind together into a hard, almost solid crust. A crust like that stops water from passing through the base at all, turning a yard that should drain in minutes into one that holds a puddle for days. Washed rock keeps those gaps open on a Oak Ridge lot long after installation, which is what lets the layer underneath keep doing its job.

The window that can melt a lawn from across the yard

Low-emissivity glass, common on newer replacement windows, reflects enough concentrated sunlight to soften a synthetic lawn from several feet away, since polyethylene blades start to give around 175 to 200°F under that kind of focused heat. The damage shows up as a scorched or melted patch in an odd shape that doesn't match any known cause until someone traces the sun's path back to a south- or west-facing window. It's worth checking any low-E glass near a Oak Ridge lawn before or after installation, since the fix, usually a window film or a repositioned pane of turf, is far cheaper than replacing a burned section later.

The order a lawn conversion actually happens in

A lawn conversion in Oak Ridge follows the same order every time regardless of yard size: strip the old sod and several inches of soil, shape the bare ground to grade, build and compact the rock base in lifts, roll out and seam the turf, then anchor the perimeter and brush in infill last. Skipping ahead, laying turf before the base has fully settled under compaction, or infilling before seams are trimmed tight, is where most callbacks trace back to later. Doing the steps in sequence, and not rushing past one to start the next, is most of what separates a lawn that holds up from one that doesn't.

What a lawn's second year actually tells you

By a Oak Ridge lawn's second year, it's been through two full rainy seasons, which is enough time for any marginal drainage or a loosely anchored edge to have already shown itself at least once. A second-year check means walking the perimeter for anything that lifted and was never caught, confirming infill still sits close to its original one to two pounds per square foot, and checking that no nearby construction or new landscaping has changed the grade the lawn was originally built to shed water toward. A lawn that's cleared two rainy seasons without incident tends to keep performing the same way afterward.

What Oak Ridge Road's history says about how old this ground is

Local records place the name Oak Ridge on this stretch of the county at least as far back as 1903, when a parcel became the cemetery that still sits at the northwest corner of Sand Lake Road and Orange Blossom Trail; county commissioners renamed several streets here in the mid-1950s, turning Macy Street into today's Oak Ridge Road. Ground that has been platted and built on that long has usually been through at least one prior landscaping cycle, sod pulled and replaced, a bed dug and filled in, which means a crew occasionally finds old irrigation line or buried debris a newer subdivision would not have. None of that changes the published price; it can add an hour or two to the strip-out on an older lot.

Questions people ask

Does turf make sense for a rental property in Oak Ridge?

For a lease that turns over every year or two, often yes: there is no mowing schedule for a tenant to skip and no sod to replace between leases. The broader cost comparison lays out the ten-year math either way.

How do you price a duplex with two separate yards?

Usually as one job with a shared seam kept off the property line, not two separate quotes. Two water meters just mean heads on each side get capped independently.
